extracted.intended_audience: aspiring journalists, newspaper editors, and students of the journalism profession
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for the practice and making of newspaper editors and journalists — the aptitudes, experience, temperament and ethical obligations that constitute successful professional journalism in the American daily press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to write and judge writing
rubrics_metrics.description: “The great editor is by no means the great writer. But he ought to be able to write and must be a judge of writing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An editor need not be the best creative writer, but must have writing ability and be able to assess and improve others' copy; being a judge of writing is a core editorial skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of every range of the newspaper office
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor 'needs to know and does know every range of it between the editorial room, the composing room and the pressroom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical familiarity with all departments of a newspaper is required so the editor can supervise effectively and understand production constraints and workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical experience and step-by-step rise
rubrics_metrics.description: The great editor should have risen, 'as it were, step-by-step from the ground floor to the roof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Career progression through the ranks (reporter, copy desk, production, etc.) is emphasized as the route to acquire practical judgment and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial leadership and control of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper office is 'a little kingdom' and the editor must 'hold well in hand everybody and every function.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong managerial skills: coordinating staff, asserting supervisory authority, and keeping the various newsroom operations aligned fall under the editor's remit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament and judgement: level-headed, yet impressionable; sympathetic, yet self-possessed; able quickly to sift, detect and discriminate
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor 'should be level-headed, yet impressionable; sympathetic, yet self-possessed; able quickly to sift, detect and discriminate; of various knowledge, experience and interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A balance of open-mindedness and steadiness, combined with rapid critical judgment and broad interests, is required for evaluating news and making editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility (valued over narrow specialism)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Assuming journalism, equally with medicine and law, to be a profession, it is the only profession in which versatility is not a disadvantage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike fields that reward narrow specialization, journalism benefits from breadth of skills and topics; versatility across roles and subjects is an advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness and ethical independence
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Disinterestedness being the soul of successful journalism, unselfish devotion to every noble purpose in public and private life, he should say to preferment, as to bribers, "get behind me, Satan."’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must resist bribery, personal aggrandizement and partisan preferment; ethical independence and public-spiritedness are central professional requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal journalism / accountability and trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Personal journalism cannot be escaped… the “one-man power” … must be clear and answerable, responsive to the common weal, and, above all, trustworthy.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a newspaper exerts one-man authority or personal journalism, that leadership must be transparent, accountable to the public, and maintain trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Print the news 'fully and fairly, without fear or favor' (timely, comprehensive reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: James Gordon Bennett's formula: printing 'the news of the day, comprising the History of Yesterday, fully and fairly, without fear or favor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News coverage should aim to be prompt, comprehensive, impartial and fearless; this is presented as the foundational editorial mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nose for news
rubrics_metrics.description: The successful journalist/editor must possess the 'nose for news'—an instinct for what is newsworthy and how to present it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate news judgment and the ability to recognize and prioritize stories of public interest; this instinct underlies much editorial success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid meretriciousness; aim for wholesome, measured content (middle of the road)
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor should 'keep to the middle of the road' and the public is 'beginning to distinguish between the wholesome and the meretricious in their newspapers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid flashy, sensational or tawdry content in favor of measured, respectable reporting that earns public confidence and long-term support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aptitude as foundational
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Aptitude, as the first ingredient, goes without saying of every line of human endeavor. We have the authority of the adage for the belief that it is not possible to make a silk purse out of a sow's ear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innate ability and talent for journalism are necessary prerequisites; training and experience matter, but basic aptitude is indispensable.
